title: Block envisions bitcoin for all
snippet: The company’s head of bitcoin, Miles Suter, has two big tasks: Make bitcoin a routine payment tool and change the global financial system.
fullText:
Block executive Miles Suter envisions a day when bitcoin is functional, everyday digital money used as easily as cards and cash for routine transactions. 

To get there, Suter – the head of bitcoin and stablecoin at Block – has set out to make payments between millions of American consumers and Square merchants happen in bitcoins.

“We’re in a unique position as a large company with huge segments on both sides of the counter,” Suter said Wednesday, alluding to U.S. consumers and merchants in Square’s point of sale ecosystem. “I believe that there’s no company in the world doing more for bitcoin than Block.”

Suter joined Block nine years ago. The company’s first bitcoin service, bitcoin sales on Cash App, launched in January 2018, with about 24 million active users purchasing the digital currency since then.

But Block has much larger aspirations for bitcoin than merely selling it. Those ambitions are driven by the company’s top executive and long-time bitcoin booster Jack Dorsey.

Enabling bitcoin payments is key, Suter said in an interview. “Jack really believes in the mission of bitcoin as everyday money, and so those are the things I’m always thinking about as we roll out new products and how they can eventually lead to that endpoint.”

To increase awareness of bitcoin, Block launched its first consumer advertising campaign last week in a bid to push the digital currency into the consciousness of what it termed “60 million bitcoin curious Americans,” a figure the company derived from an August survey it commissioned.

The video clips in Block’s “Bitcoin Does” campaign spotlight affordability issues and consumers’ frustration with issues such as inflation, merchants’ transaction fees and rising housing costs. The campaign is mainly being shown on major social media sites, like Instagram, and on Fox Sports television. Ads will also show before two major Hollywood films slated for December releases.

Dorsey, Block’s billionaire founder, has been a bitcoin enthusiast for several years and has overseen expansion of the digital asset into several areas of the company’s business. “I don’t think there is anything more important in my lifetime to work on,” Dorsey said at a 2021 bitcoin conference, CNBC reported.

Block’s effort to promote bitcoin use among consumers comes a year after the company integrated bitcoin payments into the Square point-of-sale services in October 2025. Square also allows merchants to convert part of their card sales into bitcoin.

Another Block business, Cash App, has about 59 million active users of its digital wallet, while Square counts about 4 million sellers on its system. Block offers a 5% discount in bitcoin for Cash App users who pay with the digital currency at a Square merchant.

“I don’t think anybody else has an opportunity to kick off a two-sided marketplace like this,” Suter said of the Cash App-Square interaction. “People have talked about like, ‘Well, maybe bitcoin's relevant finally when you can use it to go buy your daily coffee.’ And now, that’s definitely a reality.”

Block sees consumers’ conversion from traditional fiat money to electronic bitcoin funds as a three-part journey: accessibility to the currency through Cash App; security in its digital wallet; and daily use through Cash App consumers and Square merchants.

“We believe bitcoin needs to be money,” to make it a long-term reality, Suter said. 

In terms of bitcoin’s digital cousin, stablecoins, he considers them “a meaningful step on the long-term road towards broad-based bitcoin adoption by the world,” Suter said. Stablecoins are less volatile than bitcoins due to their 1-to-1 backing with fiat currencies.

“It gets people comfortable with this concept of a digital currency,” he said. However, he added, stablecoins “are an extension and a technological innovation of that same” financial system that operates on fiat currencies. 

That contrasts with bitcoin, which is a decentralized digital asset that has no government or central bank control and is subject to extreme price swings. 

“For me, bitcoin is a more revolutionary, upgraded system,” Suter said. “They’re not necessarily in the same ballpark.”

Stablecoin-payment efforts to date “don’t necessarily have the right posture,” he said, because a digital wallet and POS system may not locate each other or offer the proper incentives for people to try the new payment method.

“We believe in the principles of Bitcoin, and really one of the principles of bitcoin is having a really long-term time horizon, and that’s no shade to stablecoins,” Suter said. “They’re a very useful tool, especially in developing markets. And in the long run, they will assist bitcoin on its path to being everyday money.”

Block’s ecosystem of bitcoin products includes direct sales to customers and transaction revenue through Cash App; a $250 digital bitcoin wallet it launched in April; and a business unit that sells hardware and software tools for bitcoin mining. Direct sales account for the bulk of bitcoin revenues, according to Block’s annual report.

In the second quarter, Block’s gross profit from bitcoin fell 31%, to $72 million, from the same period last year due to Block’s “strategic decision” to trim fees for bitcoin purchases. It also removed fees from purchases over $2,000, and acknowledged that “bitcoin trading dynamics” in the quarter contributed to the profit decline. Block’s bitcoin revenue dipped 13% to $1.89 billion in the second quarter.

Beyond consumers’ comfort and adoption of bitcoin, merchants’ desires for a lower-cost payment rail may ultimately push wider use of the digital coins, Suter said.

“The Square side is still a bit more nascent, but when we do talk to merchants, the thing that they do key in on are those cost savings, and that is what we’ve led with in a lot of our messaging to existing and prospective merchants,” he said, noting that the current card-based system is “really good in a lot of ways.” 

“Ultimately, I do think (costly network fees) will be one of the things that helps to kickstart this, but changing the global financial system is probably the hardest thing I could imagine,” Suter said. “And so I just zoom out again, sometimes, and know that this is a really long-term journey and mission that I’m committed to and Block is committed to.”

Merchants have received about $631.7 million to date as part of a multi-billion dollar class-action lawsuit settlement with the card networks Visa and Mastercard, according to a court filing Friday.

The damages disbursements have gone to 689,340 merchants so far, including $212.8 million from a second partial distribution that began last month, class administrator Epiq said in the filing with the U.S. District Court in Brooklyn, New York.

District Judge Brian Cogan approved the second distribution in June as part of his oversight of a $5.5 billion settlement with the two largest U.S. card networks. About 84,000 merchant claimants who sued as part of the class action are covered in the second round of merchant payouts.

The settlement partially resolved an antitrust case in which merchants alleged the two network giants charged them excessive interchange fees when customers paid with a credit or debit card. The merchants’ class includes any U.S. business that accepted Visa or Mastercard-branded cards between Jan. 1, 2004, and Jan. 25, 2019. 

The settlement fund held $5.02 billion as of Sept. 30, following the distributions to merchants, according to the report by Epiq, the class administrator in the litigation. The next quarterly report to the court on claims will be filed in January.

The settlement for the damages portion of the case was reached in 2018 and received final approval by a federal judge the following year, followed by appeals. 

About 1.47 million merchants filed claims in the case as of a February 2025 deadline. About 2.12 million merchant tax identification numbers were registered as part of the overall group of business owners due a potential payout from the settlement, according to the report.

Separately, U.S. Magistrate Judge Joseph Marutollo, who is assigned to help the court in the case, last week approved Epiq’s request for $21.4 million for its administration work from April through August. 

Cogan has scheduled a hearing next month on a second part of the case, a proposed settlement that covers injunctive relief in the swipe-fee litigation. 

It is supported by the card networks and attorneys for the class of plaintiffs, with the litigation dating to October 2005. Multiple large merchants, including Walmart, Circle K and DoorDash, oppose the settlement and have urged Cogan to reject it.

title: Payments income bolsters banks
snippet: Income from card, digital and other rails has swelled to about 40% of revenue for the global bank industry, according to consulting firm McKinsey.
fullText:
Dive Brief:

The global payments industry generated $2.6 trillion in revenue last year, with North America accounting for about $700 billion, second only to Asia-Pacific, which accounted for about $1 trillion, according to a report this month from consulting firm McKinsey.

Global payments revenue rose every year from 2020 to 2025, but the rate of increase has slowed, growing just 3% between 2024 and 2025, following an average 11% gain in the prior years, the Sept. 25 report said.

As a result, revenue from payments – including card fees and interest income – has swelled since 2022 to become about 40% of banking revenue annually, the report said. The industry kicked in 41% of banking revenue last year, down slightly from 42% a year earlier.

Dive Insight:

The rate of revenue growth for the payments industry will generally slow in coming years, McKinsey predicted. The results from McKinsey’s forecast echo a similar outlook from a rival, Boston Consulting Group, put forward earlier this month.

By 2030, McKinsey expects global payments industry revenue to climb to $3.2 trillion, with North American contributing about $900 billion to the 4% annual growth rate over intervening years. 

BCG similarly projected transaction revenue will climb to $1.03 trillion by 2030, from $770 billion last year, with the rate of growth expected to decline to 6% between 2025 and 2030, down from 8% between 2019 and 2025. 

How much the payments industry revenue growth rate slows will vary by region of the world as countries diverge in the types of payments systems they’re adopting and different types of payment methods thrive, or decline, in different parts of the world. 

While card networks continue to dominate in the U.S. and Canada, as well as Western Europe, India and Brazil have shifted their populations to account-to-account systems and much of Africa has adopted phone-based systems, the report noted. China has gravitated to a mix of cards and A2A transactions. Meanwhile, stablecoins are gathering momentum in some places (Africa and China), more than others (the U.S. and the U.K.)

The revenue growth rate is expected to sink the most in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, decreasing from a 14% annual average clip during the past five years, to a 3% rate from last year through 2030, according to McKinsey. North America will experience the second-biggest slowdown, from 9% to 5%, while the Asia-Pacific region decreases from 5% to 4%. Latin America is expected to grow at the fastest rate, 7%, the report predicted.

The contracting revenue will pressure companies in the payments arena to find new avenues of growth. In any case the slower growth is expected to put pressure on profit margins.

“One clear result is that institutions relying primarily on transaction-clearing volume face increasing margin pressure,” the McKinsey report said.

Four factors have bolstered payments income over the past decade, but those forces are now ebbing, McKinsey said. They included the conversion of cash payments to higher-yielding alternatives; payments volume outpacing gross domestic product expansion; rising interest rates that pushed up interest income; and the sale of related services driven by software. Now, those elements are giving way as competition rises.

“These drivers are now leveling off, and low-cost alternative payment networks are compressing transaction margins,” the McKinsey report said.

The rise of autonomous payments as part of agentic commerce could be another blow to the payments industry, potentially undercutting card fee revenue, McKinsey said. 

At the same time, the new technology offers payments companies a path to increased operational efficiencies, by decreasing administrative work expenses and increasing software engineering productivity, the consulting firm said.

title: Hyundai Card Brings 3D Motion Design to NAVER Co-Branded Card
snippet: Hyundai Card partnered with creative collective CEKAI to translate 3D billboard motion graphics into three physical card plates for its NAVER Edition3 range. The post Hyundai Card Brings 3D Motion Design to NAVER Co-Branded Card appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Hyundai Card has launched the NAVER Hyundai Card Edition3, a co-branded credit card line developed in collaboration with CEKAI, a New York-Tokyo creative collective known for anamorphic 3D billboard work for Nike, BMW and Fendi. The release marks a deliberate departure from conventional card aesthetics, applying principles from large-format digital display design to a physical payment instrument.

The project began in mid-2025 when Hyundai Card and CEKAI started exploring how to reframe the card as a medium for motion rather than a static graphic surface. Rather than designing in two dimensions and adding a sense of depth afterwards, the teams developed the visual concept and its dynamic qualities simultaneously. Korean technology group NAVER, whose brand assets anchor the card range, provided overarching design direction throughout.

The three plates

After more than 100 design drafts, the collaboration produced three card variants. Plus is positioned around the benefits of NAVER Plus Membership. Neo uses colour gradients and geometric graphics to project what the release describes as futuristic energy. Logo Metal, the premium variant, uses motion graphic techniques to make the NAVER logo appear to shift depending on the viewing angle.

Hyundai Card’s Design Lab handled the translation from screen concept to manufactured product. Laser processing was used to render fine particle effects on the metal plate, while specialist films were applied to the two plastic cards to amplify the graphic movement. The manufacturing process required close co-ordination between the creative and technical teams to preserve the motion illusion at the scale and material constraints of a payment card.

Kota Iguchi, CEKAI’s creative director and motion designer, said: “Credit cards exist as physical plates, but we can easily imagine a future where they evolve into digital displays or take on entirely different forms. This project was incredibly exciting because of those diverse possibilities.”

Market and strategic context

The announcement is primarily a product design story rather than a financial or regulatory event, but it sits within a broader pattern worth noting. Card issuers in competitive consumer markets have invested heavily in physical card differentiation as a brand and retention tool since the mid-2010s. Metal cards, in particular, have become a signalling device across premium and super-premium segments globally, used by issuers ranging from American Express to a growing number of neobanks seeking to project credibility through tangible product design.

For Hyundai Card specifically, design is a stated strategic pillar rather than a marketing afterthought. The company holds the sole South Korean issuer partnership for Apple Pay, is the exclusive issuer of American Express Centurion card designs in the market, and in October 2024 signed a contract to license its proprietary AI platform, UNIVERSE, to Sumitomo Mitsui Card Company in Japan. That licensing deal represented a notable shift: a card issuer exporting technology rather than solely operating a domestic portfolio.

The NAVER co-brand is itself a strategically significant relationship. NAVER is South Korea’s dominant search and commerce platform, and the Edition3 card connects Hyundai Card’s issuing capabilities to one of the country’s largest loyalty and membership ecosystems. Whether the design investment translates into measurable acquisition or spend lift is not addressed in the release; the commercial metrics behind co-branded card programmes of this type are rarely disclosed at launch.

The broader question for the industry is how long physical card design remains a meaningful differentiator as contactless and digital wallet payments reduce how often cardholders physically handle or display their card. For now, issuers show little sign of retreating from premium materials and elaborate finishes, suggesting the card-as-object continues to carry brand weight even as its functional role in the payment flow diminishes.

We asked the Court to make Arthur Temlett, trading as Abacus Insurance Consultants ('Abacus'), bankrupt. This is known as sequestration in Scotland. The Sheriff granted our application on 27 August 2026.

  

            						

Emma Porter of Aver Chartered Accountants ('Aver') was appointed as trustee. She will now assess Mr Temlett’s financial affairs and seek to distribute any recovered funds to creditors.

Arthur Temlett is awaiting trial on embezzlement charges brought following an investigation by Police Scotland.

On 21 January 2025, we took action to protect consumers by stopping Arthur Temlett from carrying out any regulated activities, including acting as an insurance broker. This was because of concerns that he may have sold home and motor insurance without passing premium payments on to the insurance provider.

          

            						

  

Who to contact if you’re a customer

Customers of Abacus can contact the trustee, at Aver on:

Telephone: 0330 555 6155

Email: [email protected]

Address: PO Box 24213, Edinburgh EH1 9AT 

          

        

Information for customers 

    

      

      						I purchased home or car insurance from Abacus, what should I do?
			
    

    

						

As Abacus stopped regulated activities in January 2025, we expect that most previous policies will have expired or been renewed with another provider by now. However, if customers are concerned, they should contact their insurance providers directly to check that their insurance is valid and in place. If they are uninsured, they should arrange alternative cover immediately.

Alternative insurance can be bought directly from an insurance firm or arranged via an insurance broker. The British Insurance Brokers’ Association offers a service for customers who need help finding an authorised broker.

Anyone who believes they have paid for a policy that does not exist should report this to Police Scotland in the first instance by dialling 101 and using the crime reference number: CR/0470100/24.

Customers should also contact the trustee, using the contact details above. The trustee will explain to you what to do if you are affected.

			

  

      

      						I have an existing complaint at Abacus, what happens now?
			
    

    

						

If you’ve made a complaint against Abacus, you may have a claim if you are due any money in compensation.

You should contact the trustee for more details on how complaints or claims will be dealt with, using the contact details above.

			

  

      

      						What is the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS)?
			
    

    

						

The Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) protects consumers when UK financial services firms go out of business.

Whether you’re covered by the FSCS will depend on:

The firm.

Type of activity the firm does.

The FSCS is operationally independent of the FCA. The FSCS decides whether compensation is payable under our compensation rules.

			

  

      

      						Do I need to use a claims management company or a law firm?
			
    

    

						

For the vast majority of consumers, there is no benefit in involving a third party in reclaiming your assets.

If you use a claims management company (CMC) or law firm to assist in the return of your assets, they will likely seek a fee which may reduce what you get back.

If you are considering using a CMC or law firm to assist with the return of your assets, we suggest you first discuss this with the trustee using the contact details provided above. 

			

  

  

            						

Protecting yourself from scams

Fraudsters sometimes claim to be from legitimate firms authorised by us, or (in the case of bankruptcy) the appointed trustee.

Be wary of fraudsters pretending to be Abacus, Arthur Temlett or the trustee and asking you to pay money to get your money back.

If you get an unexpected call from someone claiming to be Abacus, Arthur Temlett or the trustee you should:

End the call straight away.

Call them back using the phone numbers above.

Find out how to protect yourself from scams, including recovery room scams.

title: Treasury taps data to fend off fraud
snippet: The U.S. department has increased its scrutiny of payments using new sources of data in an attempt to stem past ‘pay and chase’ patterns.
fullText:
The Treasury Department is increasingly using data to help prevent the U.S. government from sending payments to bad actors, Secretary Scott Bessent said this week in an update on fighting fraud.

Newly deployed safeguards, including the ability to tap additional sources of data, helped protect some $3.7 trillion in payments, the department said in an Oct. 6 press release. 

“Treasury continues to transform how the federal government protects taxpayer dollars by using better data, stronger controls, and advanced technology to stop fraud and improper payments before money goes out the door,” Bessent said in the release.

The federal government’s increased vigilance in fighting fraud comes as artificial intelligence increases the threats posed not only to government agencies, but also consumers and companies. Indeed, some industry professionals have said that the federal government has not been playing a significant enough role in helping to combat the mushrooming fraud problem.

The threat of scams, where fraudsters induce consumers, companies or other organizations, to send payments under false pretenses has become a particularly troubling issue. Americans are bilked out of $119 billion annually, according to estimates in a March report from the Consumer Federation of America that included an approximation of incidents that go unreported. 

Treasury’s increased scrutiny of government payments followed an executive order last year from President Donald Trump’s calling for a crackdown on “fraud, waste and abuse” that might affect the government’s trillions of dollars in annual payments. Trump’s predecessor, then President Joe Biden, had also sought to thwart the rising fraud.

“Financial fraud threatens the integrity of Federal programs and undermines trust in Government. Agencies’ past underinvestment in technology and longstanding challenges with access to accurate data has prevented them from more fully safeguarding taxpayer dollars against fraud and improper payments,” the White House said in that March 2025 order. 

The Treasury department contended that its fraud-fighting capabilities had improved in fiscal year 2026, which ended on Sept. 30, over the prior year, by expanding access to data that helps identify fraudulent accounts. The government added nine data sets to better verify identities for payments and to improve screening of payments.

The federal government has sought to move away from past practices that amounted to ‘pay and chase,’ in which payers find themselves in the position of making improper payments and then striving, usually in vain, to recoup losses.

As of fiscal year 2026, most federal programs now have access to the additional data sources aimed at helping to identify fraudulent accounts, up from just 4% in the prior fiscal year. The remainder of programs are expected to have the access by early in the 2027 fiscal year, the release said.

As part of the improved screening, the government stopped 13,500 payments worth $175 million that were headed to falsified identities of people who were found to be deceased, the release said. 

In the White House order, the Government Accountability Office estimated the federal government’s losses at between $233 billion and $521 billion per year due to fraud.

As consumers start using artificial intelligence to comparison shop, American Express aims to guide merchants in using the new technology.

        

            

        Published Oct. 8, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                American Express is offering business clients advice on agentic commerce. The card company hosted a “Shop & Stroll” for the Charleston, South Carolina, community on Nov. 30, 2024.
            
        
            Getty Images Entertainment via Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

American Express advised businesses in a new report this week that two-thirds of U.S. consumers are using artificial intelligence tools to compare prices for products and services, according to a survey the card company fielded to provide guidance to its clients on agentic commerce. 

About six in 10 U.S. consumers said they are likely to use AI agents to receive product and service recommendations in the next 12 months, according to results of the August survey of 2,005 adults by global advisory firm Teneo and released Tuesday.

Just over half (52%) of the respondents said they would let an AI agent buy household essentials, groceries or low-cost items, but only 15% said they would permit an AI agent to make more expensive purchases, such as electronics and appliances.

Dive Insight:

The New York card giant said it’s convening an advisory council of merchants to help advise sellers, and to incorporate input from businesses across various industries, as AI-enabled commerce progresses, per the press release. 

As more consumers turn to AI for product recommendations and bargain hunting, businesses are bracing for the impact of agentic commerce. 

Alongside the consumer survey, Amex asked 502 business leaders about the rise of agentic AI. Most (83%) of the business leaders see agentic commerce as an opportunity for their companies, but only 41% are experimenting with or integrating the technology into their operations.

That gap might be explained by the speed at which agentic commerce is evolving. Nearly two-thirds (64%) of businesses surveyed said staying abreast of the rapidly evolving technology is a challenge. The majority (86%) of the business respondents expect they will need some support from payment providers and partners to prep their businesses for the agentic AI shift. 

“We believe agentic commerce could be the most significant change in shopping and purchasing behavior since the start of e-commerce,” Amex group president of global merchant and network services, Anna Marrs, said in a press release. “We’re focused on helping businesses understand what’s changing, prepare for what’s next and capture the opportunities ahead.”

In addition to canvassing consumers and companies about their perceptions of agentic AI, American Express is preparing for shopping mishaps that could happen with the technology. Earlier this year, the company said it would protect consumers from accidental AI purchases, subject to its terms and conditions.

title: Finance leaders fight deepfakes
snippet: Corporate finance departments are grappling with AI-enabled fraud, according to the results of a new survey by Early Warning Services’ Certos.
fullText:
Encountering fraud that looks like the workings of an artificial intelligence tool? You’re not alone.

According to a new survey of 230 senior financial leaders conducted by Early Warning Services’ fraud prevention unit Certos, as many as 81% of respondents said their company had experienced an attempted fraud that involved, or appeared to involve, “AI-generated or AI-enhanced content or techniques” within the last year.

A similar share (79%) said they were very concerned that AI-enabled fraud could negatively affect trust in their organization.

The potential repercussions of AI-powered fraud, evidently, are sweeping. In response to an open-ended question about their biggest concerns about AI-enabled fraud or scams, just about one in five respondents (21%) cited the potential for executive deepfake impersonation. The most common response to that question, cited by 43% of respondents, was payment diversion, followed by detection gaps or control lags, named by 38% of respondents.

As one anonymous CFO of a Fortune 500 company put it: “Biggest concern is a convincing fake request slipping through and sending company money to the wrong place.Certos conducted the online survey Aug. 7-21 and received 79 responses from leaders at Fortune 500 companies, 127 from venture-backed companies and 24 from charitable organizations. The survey didn’t include responses from banks and credit unions, investment managers, financial services or fintech firms or those working on AI model development or AI services.

Detection gaps

Fraudsters who use AI may be likelier to slip through the cracks, too. Eighty-four percent of respondents said that AI-enabled fraud is much, or somewhat more difficult, to detect than traditional fraud. And, where most respondents (87%) believed they were very, or somewhat, prepared for the “sophistication of AI-enabled fraud and scams,” only half were confident they could identify such fraud or scam attempts “before money leaves the organization.”

Certos’ report comes at a time when businesses across many industries continue to loudly and enthusiastically embrace new AI tools in the name of productivity, even as purveyors of the technology themselves continue to issue dire warnings about the threats posed by their own products. In a leaked prospectus document obtained by Reuters, for instance, Anthropic officials explicitly said that advanced AI could lead to “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

In an email, a Certos spokesperson acknowledged that “AI can make fraud easier to create, scale and disguise.”

“But the bigger takeaway from the research is that this is becoming a commercial banking issue, not simply a cybersecurity issue,” the spokesperson said. “More broadly, we do not view these findings as a reason to retreat from technology. They show that the threat is evolving quickly and that financial institutions need to continue evolving their defenses along with it.”

Executives are certainly not the only ones facing AI-related fraud, with recent research by Consumer Reports showing that nine in 10 Americans have encountered at least one type of cyberattack or digital scam. “Scams are felt by everyone and rapidly evolving thanks to AI,” said Craig Newmark, founder of Craigslist and the “Take 9” cybersecurity public awareness campaign, in that report.

In a world of compounding fraud, driven by AI or otherwise, whose job is it to stop such incursions? The Certos report suggests that companies are increasingly leaning on their financial institutions for some help. Ninety-three percent of respondents said that AI-enabled fraud risk is changing how their organization thinks about its financial institution partners.

When asked to name their top three expectations of their financial institutions, more than half (51%) of respondents said they’re looking for “better detection of suspicious activity.” Early Warning Services is owned by some of the top banks in the U.S.

In a statement, Certos General Manager Ben Chance said that the solution to AI-enabled fraud rests on “having the inter-bank network intelligence to help determine whether the receiving account actually belongs to the person or business the sender thinks they’re paying before money leaves the bank.”

In an email, a Certos spokesperson pointed out that the survey shows “strong agreement that this problem cannot be solved by any one institution or sector alone.”

Response to fraud, the spokesperson said, has to “extend across the ecosystem.”

“Telecom providers, payment networks, marketplaces, law enforcement, regulators and policymakers all have roles to play,” the spokesperson said.

Early Warning Services officially launched Certos in April in an effort to solidify and rebrand the company’s fraud prevention efforts. “The industry is at this point where we really, as an industry, need to reinvest in our fraud tools and our fraud capabilities and keep up with the pace of innovation that we’re seeing from threat actors,” Chance said in an interview at that time.

title: Bahrain central bank to treble tech budget
snippet: The Central Bank of Bahrain (CBB) plans to increase its investment in technology by threefold over the next three years as part of a plan to develop Bahrain to the region's primary banking hub.
